actions.reason: After reading b58encode and lineage_bench.py I found no change likely to reach a 1% encode_ir gain, so I made no edits and ran no evaluations. My rough estimates (not measured): encode calls are about 10% of the counted instructions, and the long 256-1024 byte blobs about 3%. Switching to a base**5 divisor (the largest power of 58 that still fits in one internal int digit) would cut long-blob division work by about 20%, which is about 0.5% overall. On 32- and 64-byte inputs it would cost more, because each group of five characters needs more small-int operations and lookups. A three-character table would cost too much to build. Splitting large numbers into halves first, or parallel division across byte lanes, doesn't help with CPython's quadratic division, or would need complex and unreadable code. The encode table build is under 0.4% of the total. Earlier measurements showed that added code costs instructions at module load and that C iterator chains are slower, so small per-call tweaks aren't worth an evaluation.

journal.text:
Test agent here. I read base58/__init__.py, lines 1 to 324, and lineage_bench.py, lines 1 to 92. I looked hardest at b58encode and at how the bench counts instructions. The bar was a 1% encode_ir gain with the same bytes out.

I made no edits and ran no evaluations. I stopped without submitting a candidate. My notes hold rough shares, and none of them is measured. Encode calls look like about 10% of counted instructions. The long 256-1024 byte blobs look like about 3%. Not measured yet.

What I believe now: the encode loop does one big-int divmod per output char. A base**5 divisor could do one per five chars. That is the largest power of 58 that fits in one internal int digit. But long blobs are a thin slice of the total. Even a good cut there looks like a small ripple against the 1% line.

Next step: run the bench as it stands and measure the real encode share before writing any code.
